title: Words That Never Were
description: Dord, the dictionary's ghost word; Mountweazels and trap streets; and eight buffalo in a row

concepts.title: Dord: A Word Made by a Filing Slip
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1934 Merriam-Webster published Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition, a 17-pound giant that took 250 editors and consultants to make. Among its entries was dord, a word meaning "density". It had no etymology and no example of anyone ever using it, and Merriam-Webster's own files held no evidence for it either.1

The trouble began with a 3x5 slip typed up by the chemistry editor, Austin M. Patterson. It was one of several slips for things the letter D can stand for, and it read "D or d": capital or lowercase d, both abbreviations for density. But slips for headwords were typed with spaces between all the letters, to leave room for marks showing stress and syllable breaks. So whoever handled this one saw a four-letter word with one space missing, and underlined all four letters to be set in bold as a headword. A pronunciation was added, and the word slipped past every later reader.2

In 1939 an editor spotted the error and wrote a slip marked "Imperative, urgent!", yet the correction did not reach print until 1947.3 Lexicographers have a name for a word born of an error and never really used: a ghost word, which Merriam-Webster defines as "a word form never in established usage".4

The blunder shows how a dictionary is meant to work. A word earns its place through evidence: examples of it in published, edited text, kept in the publisher's files. Dord had no evidence at all, and Merriam-Webster counts it as its only ghost word.5

concepts.title: Mountweazels and Trap Streets
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia remembers Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer famous for Flags Up!, her pictures of rural American mailboxes. Born in Bangs, Ohio, in 1942, she died at 31 in an explosion while on assignment for Combustibles magazine. She never existed. "It was an old tradition in encyclopedias to put in a fake entry to protect your copyright," one of its editors, Richard Steins, told The New Yorker in 2005.1

The same article went hunting for a newer Mountweazel, as it called such fakes. The 2001 New Oxford American Dictionary defines esquivalience as "the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities". Its editor-in-chief, Erin McKean, confirmed it was invented to protect the copyright of the electronic version. It had already turned up on Dictionary.com.2

Mapmakers have it harder, because a copier can claim to have simply described the same real world. So in the 1930s Otto G. Lindberg of the General Drafting Company and his assistant, Ernest Alpers, put an invented hamlet, Agloe, on an empty dirt road in their New York State map, its name built from their initials. When Agloe turned up on a Rand McNally map, the story goes, the rival had an answer: a general store on the spot had taken the name from a map, so Agloe now existed.3

Fakes like this are known as trap streets. One suspected example, Lye Close in Bristol, appears on an A-Z street map but not in its index, or in reality. Publishers rarely admit to them. When Britain's Ordnance Survey accused the Automobile Association of copying, it pointed to design quirks such as road widths rather than planted fakes, and in 2001 the AA agreed to pay it £20 million.4

concepts.title: Eight Buffalo Make a Sentence
concepts.contentHtml:
Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo. It looks like a stuck key, but it is grammatical English, because buffalo can do three jobs. It is a city in western New York. It is an animal, whose plural can be plain "buffalo". And it is a verb meaning to intimidate, or to confuse or deceive.1

Add the missing words and the structure appears: Buffalo buffalo [that] Buffalo buffalo buffalo, buffalo Buffalo buffalo. Bison from Buffalo, whom other Buffalo bison bully, themselves bully Buffalo bison. Two habits of English make this work. A place name can sit in front of a noun as a modifier, as in "Boston cats". And English lets you drop "that" from a relative clause, so "mice that cats chase eat cheese" can shrink to "Mice cats chase eat cheese". With every "that" gone and every word identical, the reader gets no clue where one phrase ends and the next begins.2

The sentence has several inventors. In 1972 William J. Rapaport, then a philosophy graduate student at Indiana University, heard his professor John Tienson offer "Dogs dogs dog dog dogs" as an example, and came up with a five-buffalo version, later stretched to ten. Steven Pinker printed the eight-word version in The Language Instinct in 1994, crediting his student Annie Senghas, and the computational linguist Robert Berwick recalled meeting the sentence as a child, before 1972.3

Carl de Marcken of MIT's AI Lab used such sentences to test computer parsers. In a joking note he worked out that, under his small grammar, each extra buffalo multiplies the number of possible readings by about 1.33.4

title: Languages That Break the Rules
description: Pirahã's missing numbers, Guugu Yimithirr's compass talk, and Rotokas's six consonants

concepts.title: Pirahã: No Word for One
concepts.contentHtml:
For a study published in 2008, a team from MIT, with the linguist Daniel Everett translating, set out spools of thread in front of speakers of Pirahã, a small hunter-gatherer people of the Brazilian Amazon, and asked how many there were. Adding spools one at a time up to ten, speakers used three words, hói, hoí and baágiso, which looked like "one", "two" and "many". But when the team started at ten and took spools away, hói was used for as many as six. The team concluded that Pirahã has no way at all to express an exact quantity, not even one.1

Yet the speakers could match exact amounts. Laying out balloons to match a row of spools, they got 54 of 56 trials right. With the spools hidden behind a folder, they got only 24 of 56. Number words, the authors argued, are not needed for the idea of an exact quantity; they are a cognitive technology for remembering one.2

Everett had made a bolder claim in 2005: that their language shows no recursion, the tucking of one phrase inside another of the same type, as in "the man who is wearing a top hat". Pirahã, he said, strings separate sentences instead: "I saw the dog. The dog was at the beach. A snake bit the dog." That cut against Noam Chomsky, who had argued that recursion is the cornerstone of all languages.3

Andrew Nevins, David Pesetsky and Cilene Rodrigues reread Everett's own earlier descriptions and reported "strong syntactic and semantic evidence" that Pirahã does have embedded clauses.4 A 2016 corpus study, with Everett among its authors, found no unambiguous embedding but called its conclusions "highly tentative". Part of the quarrel is over definitions: in the broad sense Nevins and colleagues use, any sentence over two words long is recursive.5

concepts.title: Guugu Yimithirr: East, Not Left
concepts.contentHtml:
When the late Tulo Gordon was translating traditional Guugu Yimithirr stories into English with the anthropologist John Haviland, he reached a lagoon that lies, as his language puts it, west of the Cooktown airport. "But white fellows wouldn't understand that," he said. "In English we'd better say, 'to the right as you drive to the airport'."1

Guugu Yimithirr (also spelled Guugu Yimidhirr) is spoken at Hopevale, near Cooktown in far north Queensland. Its speakers describe position and motion with four roots close to north, south, east and west: gungga, jiba, naga and guwa. Each names a quadrant rather than a point, and the whole set is turned slightly clockwise from the compass.2

The popular claim that the language has no words for left and right goes too far: it does distinguish a left hand from a right hand. What it never does is locate things by left and right. Instead of the cup on your left, it is the cup to the north, whichever way you face, so speakers must always know their bearings. Inspired partly by this language, the linguist Stephen Levinson sorted spatial systems into three frames: intrinsic ("at the foot of the bed"), relative ("to the right of the tree") and absolute ("north of the tree").3

The language also gave English a famous word. In 1770 James Cook's Endeavour spent weeks at the Endeavour River under repair after striking a reef, and the crew wrote down more than a hundred local words. One was gangurru, a large black or grey kangaroo, which Cook recorded as "Kanguroo".4 The tale that "kangaroo" means "I don't understand" is a myth. It grew later, partly because people around Sydney, far to the south, used other names for the animal.5

concepts.title: Rotokas: Six Consonants Will Do
concepts.contentHtml:
In the jungle of Bougainville, the ornithologist Jared Diamond listened as a guide from the village of Rotokas named the local birds: kópipi, kurupi, vokupi, kopikau, kororo, keravo. The only consonants in those names were k, p, r and v. Diamond later learned that the Rotokas language has just six consonant sounds, yet its speakers, 4,320 at the last count he had in 1993, build a rich vocabulary and communicate clearly.1

The World Atlas of Language Structures, surveying 566 languages, found consonant inventories from 6 to 122, with Rotokas, of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea, at the bottom. In phonetic shorthand its six can be written p, t, k, b, d, g, though each covers a wide range of pronunciations. At the top is !Xóõ of Botswana, with 122, mostly because of its many click sounds. English has 24, close to the typical figure in the low twenties.2

Rotokas also has no nasal consonants, no m and no n, and makes no systematic use of nasal sounds at all. Pirahã, from the first story, shares that gap, and both have especially small sound systems overall.3 Guinness World Records lists the Rotokas alphabet as the shortest anywhere, with just 11 letters.4

Extremes like this test an old idea: that every language is equally complex overall, so simplicity in one part must be paid for with complexity somewhere else. If sound systems do not trade off that way, writes the atlas's author Ian Maddieson, the reasonable conclusion is that languages with quite different levels of complexity function just as well as each other.5

title: Talking Without Words
description: Whistled Spanish on La Gomera, drums that speak in tones, and an island where everyone signed

concepts.title: The Island That Whistles
concepts.contentHtml:
On a cliff on La Gomera, in the Canary Islands, Antonio Márquez Navarro whistles an invitation across a ravine: come over, we are going to slaughter the pig. Three hikers in the distance stop dead at the piercing sound, then walk on, none the wiser. In his youth, he says, shepherds on the island's steep paths would have whistled an answer straight back.1

This is Silbo Gomero, Spanish carried entirely in whistles. Whistles carry: whistled speech can be understood up to ten times as far away as a shout, and on La Gomera a few shepherds still whistle to each other across valleys that would take hours to cross.2

Silbo is not a code of agreed signals. It is Spanish, rebuilt sound by sound. In the standard description, two distinct whistles stand in for the five Spanish vowels and four for the consonants, told apart by pitch and by whether the whistle runs on or breaks off.3 The brain treats it as language, too. In a 2005 brain-imaging study, listening to Silbo activated the brain areas normally used for spoken language in skilled whistlers, but not in people who could not whistle it.4

With so few sounds, some words collide: gallina (hen) and ballena (whale) whistle the same, so only the rest of the sentence tells a listener which animal is meant. In 2009 UNESCO added Silbo to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Now that nobody needs it to send news, its survival rests mostly on a 1999 law that made it a compulsory subject in the island's schools.5

concepts.title: Drums That Talk
concepts.contentHtml:
In his first months as a Baptist missionary in the Belgian Congo, John Carrington walked with a colleague to a forest village. They had sent no messenger ahead, yet the teacher, the medical assistant and the church members were all waiting in the schoolroom. The last village had sent word ahead by drum.1

Carrington's book Talking Drums of Africa (1949) explained the trick. Many Central African languages are tonal: every syllable is either high or low, and the tone is part of the word. A wooden slit drum gives two notes, high and low, depending on where it is struck, and skin drums are played in high and low pairs. So the drums copy the tone pattern of real words.2

That raises a problem, because many words share a pattern. Among the Lokele people, whose drums Carrington studied, the words for manioc, plantain, above and forest all have identical tones and rhythm. So a drummer never beats a word alone. Each noun comes wrapped in a longer stock phrase whose pattern is unique, which removes the ambiguity: money is "the pieces of metal which arrange palavers", and the moon is always "the moon looks down at the earth".3 Messages get longer, but they travel: a Lokele drum usually carries about six or seven miles at night and four or five by day.4

In West Africa, Yoruba drummers speak on the dùndún, a drum whose skin is tightened by squeezing its tuning cords. Yoruba has three tones, so the drummer sets the skin loose for a low tone, half-tight for mid and tight for high, and can bend the pitch while the skin is still ringing to copy the glides of speech.5

concepts.title: Everyone Here Signed
concepts.contentHtml:
Old islanders in Chilmark, on Martha's Vineyard, had stories to tell: of children signing behind the schoolteacher's back, adults signing to each other during sermons, farmers signing to their children across a wide field and fishermen signing from their boats.1

Deafness ran in Chilmark families. In 1854 the national average was one deaf person in every 5,728; in Chilmark it was one in 25. Alexander Graham Bell came to investigate, dismissed local theories that blamed a mother's fright or clay from the Gay Head cliffs, and concluded that the deafness was inherited.2

With deaf people in so many families, sign language became everybody's language. Nora Ellen Groce's 1985 book, Everyone Here Spoke Sign Language, found that many hearing islanders signed, sometimes even when no deaf person was present. Linguists now call such a language a village sign language, and others survive today: in one Balinese village, some 57% of hearing villagers have at least some skill in the local sign language.3

Groce pictured a remote community that grew up on its own for about 133 years until 1825. A 2024 study of historical, demographic and family records argues that it began in Chilmark in 1785, 93 years later than previously thought, and had only about 40 years to itself before deaf education connected it to the young signing community of New England.4 The end came through marriage. As members of old island families married off-islanders, the gene pool widened, and by 1952 the last of the known hereditary deaf on the island had died.5

title: Myths, Mysteries and OK
description: The Eskimo snow-word myth, twins with a 'secret language', and a Boston joke that gave us OK

concepts.title: How Many Words for Snow?
concepts.contentHtml:
It is one of the most repeated claims about language: Eskimos have dozens, even hundreds, of words for snow. In 1984 alone the number was given as nine in a trivia encyclopedia, a hundred in a New York Times editorial and two hundred in a Cleveland TV weather forecast.1

The trail leads back to Franz Boas, in the introduction to a 1911 handbook on American Indian languages. His point was modest: just as English has separate roots for lake, river and brook, Eskimo has apparently separate roots for snow on the ground (aput), falling snow (qana), drifting snow (piqsirpoq) and a snowdrift (qimuqsuq): four roots in all.2 In 1940 Benjamin Lee Whorf, a fire-prevention inspector and weekend linguist, retold it in an MIT magazine,3 and the list grew with every retelling. Geoffrey Pullum lampooned the result in his 1989 essay "The Great Eskimo Vocabulary Hoax", written to publicize the anthropologist Laura Martin's work on the myth.4

Yet the snow words are real; the hard part is counting them. Inuit and Yupik languages are polysynthetic: suffixes pile onto a base word, so one Siberian Yupik word can mean "what's more, he wants a bigger boat", and a dictionary maker must decide which forms count as separate words. Counting carefully, the Smithsonian anthropologist Igor Krupnik and colleagues found 40 snow terms in Central Siberian Yupik and at least 53 in the Inuit of Nunavik, in Canada, including pukak, powder snow that looks like salt.5 So the famous numbers were invented, but the real vocabulary is large, and its size depends on what counts as a word.

concepts.title: Poto and Cabengo
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1977 six-year-old twins arrived at the language clinic of Children's Hospital in San Diego. Their talk, the director said, sounded "as if a tape recorder were turned on fast forward with an occasional understandable word jumping out."1

Grace and Virginia Kennedy, who called each other Poto and Cabengo, became the best-known case of cryptophasia, or twin language. After convulsions in infancy, their parents decided they were permanently disabled (later tests found roughly normal IQs) and kept them indoors, away from other children, with a grandmother who left them to themselves. At six they spoke no English, only what was reported as a sophisticated private language of their own.2

Then linguists slowed the tapes down. Richard Meier and Elissa Newport found that the apparent hundreds of new words were about 50 complex, mispronounced words and phrases, jammed together at high speed; a baffling word for spaghetti, toolaymeia, was "O sole mio". Their verdict: "deformed English".3 Most of it was English, with some German, the other language at home: "Liba Cabingoat, it" meant "Dear Cabengo, eat", and they seem to have had at least 16 ways of saying "potato salad".4

Private twin talk is common; invented languages are not. A study following twins and closely spaced siblings from 20 to 36 months found "secret language" in both, far more often in twins, usually as a passing stage of immature speech in the second year that faded over the following months. A few children, mostly boy twins, kept a private language at three, and the four who never developed normal language alongside it still had poor language at about six.5

concepts.title: Oll Korrect
concepts.contentHtml:
There may be more stories about where OK came from than ways to use it: the Haitian port of Aux Cayes, Choctaw okeh, Scots och aye, Wolof waw kay, Greek olla kalla, even bakers' initials on biscuits. The truth was dug out by Allen Walker Read, a Columbia professor who scoured old sources for years and published his findings in journal articles in 1963 and 1964. As Allan Metcalf, who wrote a book on the word, puts it, OK was "born as a lame joke perpetrated by a newspaper editor in 1839."1

The joke ran in the Boston Morning Post on March 23, 1839, as part of an elaborate tease aimed at another editor, and OK stood for "all correct".2 It fitted a newspaper fad for comic abbreviations, many of them for deliberate misspellings: "no go" became K.G., for "know go"; "all right" became O.W., for "oll wright"; and "all correct" became O.K., for "oll korrect".3

Most such jokes died; OK was rescued by politics. Martin Van Buren came from Kinderhook, New York, and was nicknamed Old Kinderhook, so early in the 1840 election OK Clubs sprang up. An opponent also claimed that Andrew Jackson had been a terrible speller who marked the papers he approved O.K. for "all correct". Metcalf calls that a total hoax, but within 20 years people were writing OK on documents, and telegraph operators took it up.4

The campaign hijacked the origin story too: some people still believe OK began as Old Kinderhook. Rival ancestors piled up, and the most persistent, Choctaw okeh, was proposed in 1885. Woodrow Wilson believed it, writing okeh on papers he approved; asked why not O.K., he replied, "Because it is wrong."5
